column2: She found no comfort in food, in bed or in sleep; she was sprinkled daily by thousands of friends with cooling remedies.
Burning again and again and distressed again, she found no relief from the pain of the mighty fire of love.
Parvati, tormented by separation, could not sleep; by the burning of her own body she increased her father's grief.
Seeing his daughter's separation from Shiva, for which there was no remedy, the king of mountains felt great sorrow.
Dear one, please the god Maheshvara by austerity and obtain him as your husband. Thus urged by her father,
on a peak of the Himalaya called Gaurishikhara, Parvati performed hard austerities to obtain a husband.
In the cold seasons standing in water, in summer amid fires, with her gaze fixed on the sun, she undertook very severe austerities.
Pleased by that very austerity, Shiva granted her his presence and accepted her as his wife according to the rite of marriage.
Then he married the lotus-eyed daughter given by the lord of mountains, whom he had earlier sought through the Seven Sages.
Enjoying himself with her for a long time, Maheshvara lived in his father-in-law's house in the city of Oshadhiprastha.
Returning again to Kailasa with all the Pramathas, he brought Parvati there, giving joy to the lord of mountains.
Enjoying himself with her on Kailasa and on Mandara, on the Vindhya, the golden mountain, Malaya and Pariyatraka,
in various places Maheshvara found delight. Then he released his fierce seed into her, which she could not bear.
She cast it on the earth; it was thrown into fire and into the Krittikas; they released it into the waters of the Ganga, and she into a forest of reeds.
There arose the great hero Mahasena, the six-faced one; he was brought to the Ganga, and the matted-haired god rejoiced.
Growing day by day, of fierce valour, taught by his own father, he acquired all knowledge.
Then, with his father's permission, becoming commander of the gods' army, he slew Taraka together with all the Danavas.
Then Guha married Devasena, given by Shakra, who was delighted by the slaying of Taraka, lord of the Daityas.
That glorious daughter of Shakra named Devasena, obtaining Skanda as her husband, felt great joy.
Having thus bewitched the whole circle of the universe and accomplished the work of the gods, the mind-born god went back to Shripura.
To that holy city of Shri, where Lalita the supreme Queen abides for the prosperity of the worlds, he went to serve her.
Therefore the circumference at the base of the gate-tower is twenty yojanas; above that, the circumference is declared to decrease.
The height of the gate-tower is said to be twenty-five yojanas; at every yojana there is a charming door with panels.
The storeys are as many, decreasing as they rise; the top of the gate-tower extends a yojana.
Its length is the same, and there it is said to have three crowns; the width of each crown is a krosha, O pot-born one.
It rises two kroshas, decreasing like the gate-tower, O sage; the ground between the crowns measures half a krosha.
On the eastern and southern gate-towers the crowns face west; on the western gate-tower the crowns face south and north.
The crowns of the northern gate are declared like those of the southern gate; on the eastern gate the crowns are arranged like those of the western gate.
Within the wall called Kalayasa, seven yojanas in, is the bronze wall with gate-towers as before.
The measure of the base of the wall is declared as before; the bronze wall too has gates in the east and the other directions,
and at every gate there are gate-towers with the same features. The region between the iron and bronze walls all around
is said to be a great garden of various trees, O pot-born one; everything that springs from the earth is found there.
More than thousands of trees, ever in flower and ever in fruit, ever beautiful with fresh shoots, ever full of fragrance:
mangoes, kankolas, lodhras, bakulas, karnikaras, shimshapas, shirishas, devadarus and nameru trees,
punnagas, nagabhadras, muchukundas, katphalas, cardamoms, cloves, takkolas and camphor trees,
pilus, kakatundis, shalakas, asanas, kanchanaras, lakuchas, jackfruits and hingulas,
patalas, phalinis, jatilis, jaghanephalas, ganikas, kurantas, bandhujivas and pomegranates,
ashvakarnas, hastikarnas, champakas, golden trees, jasmines, talaparnis and ever-fruiting tulasis,
palmyras, tamalas, hintalas, date palms, sharas, barburas, sugarcanes, milky trees, shleshmantakas and vibhitakas,
haritakis, avakpushpis, ghontalis, svargapushpikas, bhallatakas, khadiras, shakhotas and sandal trees,
black aloe trees, kalaskandhas, tamarinds and vatas, udumbaras, arjunas, ashvatthas, shami trees and dhruva trees,
ruchakas, kutajas, saptaparnas, kritamalakas, kapitthas and tintinis — thousands of such trees,
pervaded by the various seasons, causes of the Goddess's delight; excellent trees of many kinds and great height stand there.
Within the bronze wall, seven yojanas in, is the square copper wall, rising seven yojanas.
The ground between these two is called the Kalpaka garden; the trees there bear fruits with the scent of camphor, containing lovely jewel-seeds,
very beautiful with golden skins; the fresh shoots on the branches are divine yellow garments;
their sap is nectar and their flowers are ornaments. Many such wish-fulfilling trees are said to be there.
This is the second enclosure, called Kalpavapi by name. Within the copper wall the Naga wall is declared.
The space between these two is seven yojanas; there is the Santana garden, shaped like the Kalpavapi.
The ground between them is called the Harichandana garden, like the Kalpa garden, crowded with fruits and flowers.
In all these walls the gates are arranged as before, and the gate-towers and crowns are arranged as before.
The gate-towers and doors are arranged, with equal measure at every gate. Within the Arakuta wall, seven yojanas in,
is a wall made of five metals, shaped like the previous wall; the ground between them is called the Mandara tree garden.
Within the five-metal wall, seven yojanas in, is declared the silver wall, with the characteristics described before.
The ground between them is called the Parijata tree garden, full of divine fragrance and bright with loads of fruits and flowers.
Within the silver wall, seven yojanas in, is declared the golden wall, adorned with gates as before.
The ground between them is called the Kadamba tree garden; there are divine nipa trees two yojanas high,
ever dripping with wine, bright with thick blossoms, from which comes the Yogini named Kadambari, giver of enjoyment.
That special wine-garden is ever dear to the Mantrini. Those nipa trees give good shade, are leafy and full of shoots, their interiors filled with the humming of rows of bees roaming for fragrance.
There is the very charming mansion of the Mantrinatha. In the Kadamba forest garden, in the intermediate directions beginning with the south-east,
four lofty mansions were built by the primal architect; each house is five yojanas wide,
five yojanas long, and stands within seven enclosures. So it is in the other intermediate directions, with priyaka trees everywhere. This is declared to be the residential city of Shyama.
Another city, for the army, is in the region of the great lotus forest. Since her house here is many yojanas away,
the Mantrini could not perform daily service to the Goddess; therefore a dwelling for that glorious Mantranatha was built near the house of the wish-granting gem by the divine artisan and Maya.
Who could describe the many excellences of the Mantrini Goddess's mansion in Shripura, even with a thousand tongues?
There the honoured daughters of Matanga, their eyes coppery with Kadambari wine, sing to the sweet lute and play.
Agastya said: Who is this Matanga, and how do his daughters, ever languid with the intoxication of wine, serve the Mantrinatha?
Hayagriva said: Matanga was an ascetic, a veritable heap of austerity, endowed with great power and eager to create a world.
By the power of austerity and firm mind he extended his command everywhere. His son Matanga propitiated Mudrini, the leader of mantras,
with exceedingly terrible austerities, being of steady mind. Long worshipped by the son of the sage Matanga,
the Mantrini granted him her presence and said, "Choose a boon." Then Matanga, best of all sages, a treasure of austerity, spoke to Shyamalamba, who had appeared before him.
The great sage Matanga said: O Goddess, by merely remembering you all perfections have come to me — minuteness and the rest and all other powers.
There is nothing left for me to attain in the three worlds, O Mother, for I have obtained everything through remembrance of your deeds.
Yet let this presence of yours not be fruitless for us. I ask this one boon; fulfil it, O Mother.
Long ago, in friendship and jest with Himavan, he, intoxicated with play, boasted there in unseemly words;
he praised himself saying, "I am the father of Gauri." I had no answer, since in that respect his merit was greater.
When two friends are equal in merit, and one gains greater merit for some reason, the other feels a longing.
Though my desires are fulfilled, I performed austerities to be able to boast of being the father of Gauri. So, O Mantrinatha, become my daughter,
so that you will become famous by my name, without doubt." Hearing these words of the great sage Matanga, she said "So be it" and vanished, and the sage was pleased.
Then in a dream she joyfully gave the great sage Matanga a single spray of tapichchha from her ear-ornament.
By the power of that dream, Matanga's wife, named Siddhimati, bore Laghushyama in her womb.
From her was born Matangi, hence so named; she is called Laghushyama, the root and source of Shyama.
The lovely daughters of Matanga, crores upon crores, with groups of Laghushyama, Mahashyama and Matangi, having become the limb-Shaktis, serve Priyakapriya.
Thus, O pot-born one, the origin of the daughters of Matanga has been told, and the seven enclosures and walls made of iron and other metals.
There abides, O subduer of the Vindhya, the rainy season, giver of delight to the three worlds. Nabhahshri, Nabhasyashri, Svara, Svarasva, Svamalini,
Amba, Dula, Nirali, Abhrayanti, Meghayantrika, Varshayanti, Chibunika and Varidhara are the Shaktis —
twelve declared as rain-givers, their eyes red with intoxication. With these Shaktis the rainy season
ever worships the supreme Goddess with circles of flowers born of itself, adorning the lands of Lalita's devotees with its bounty.
But afflicting the land of her enemies with drought, the coming of the clouds always abides as the Goddess's servant.
In the Mandara garden the autumn season always dwells; that glorious one, who gladdens the minds of people, guards that enclosure.
Ishashri and Urjashri are the beloved queens of that season; with them it brings water, and with circles of flowers born of itself worships the empress, the consort of Kameshvara.
The winter season, of great splendour, its body cool with snow, ever bright of face, a beloved servant of Lalita,
worshipping the supreme Goddess with masses of flowers born of itself, the tormentor of fire guards the Parijata garden.
Sahahshri and Sahasyashri are its two lovely wives. The guardian of the Kadamba forest garden is of the form of the cool season.
The cool season abides there, O best of sages, O pot-born one; by it that enclosure is made cool everywhere.
Dwelling there, Shyama is a deity of cool form. Tapahshri and Tapasyashri are its two excellent wives; with them it worships Mother Lalita, purifier of the universe.
Agastya said: O horse-faced one, glorious one, I have learned of Mahakala, guardian of the first garden among the seven of various trees,
and you have described his chakra with four enclosures. I have heard from you that the other six seasons guard the wish-tree gardens, but I have not heard of the goddesses of their chakras.
Therefore, O Lord, tell me in order the enclosure-deities of the chakras of spring and the others, for you are great and all-knowing.
Hayagriva said: Hear, O best of sages, the deities stationed in each chakra.
The Kala chakra was described before; now the chakra of spring is told: a triangle, a pentagon, an eight-petalled lotus, a sixteen-petalled lotus, and two ten-spoked figures,
and a square — it should be known as having seven enclosures. In its centre, in the dot-chakra, is the season of spring, of great radiance.
Clinging to him on either side are Madhushri and Madhavashri; with his two hands he presses one breast of each,
and with another pair of hands he holds a fragrant cup full of flower-wine and a piece of meat.

Such is the meditation on all the seasons, O slayer of the Vindhya. In the meditation on the rainy season, the first pair of Shaktis should be known as seated on the lap, and the other Shaktis near by.
Now hear as I tell the goddesses stationed in the spring chakra: the first of the bright fortnight of Madhu, the second of the bright fortnight of Madhu,
the third, the fourth, the fifth and the sixth of the bright fortnight of Madhu,
the seventh, the eighth, the ninth and the tenth of the bright fortnight of Madhu,
the eleventh, the twelfth, the thirteenth and the fourteenth of the bright fortnight of Madhu,
the full moon of Madhu; then the first, second and third of the dark fortnight of Madhu,
the fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh of the dark fortnight of Madhu,
the eighth, ninth and tenth of the dark fortnight of Madhu, O destroyer of the Vindhya's pride,
the eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth and fourteenth of the dark fortnight of Madhu,
and the new moon of Madhu — these thirty should be known as Shaktis. In the same manner, those of the month Madhava are situated around:
another thirty Shaktis beginning with the first of the bright fortnight; together, sixty are known as the Shaktis of spring.
There in the chakra they are to be worshipped by rule with their own mantras. The seven enclosure-levels of the royal spring chakra
hold sixty deities stationed on those sixty places; practitioners should worship them separately with their respective mantras.
As the spring chakra is, so are the other three; but the deities differ, according to the months Shukra, Shuchi and the rest.
Sixty mighty Shaktis are counted in the summer chakra; likewise in the rainy-season and other chakras, distinguished by Nabhas, Nabhasya and so on,
sixty Shaktis are established in each chakra; but for fear of lengthening the text I refrain from enumerating them.
These Shaktis of the seasons give happiness to Lalita's devotees, devoted to Lalita's worship, meditation, recitation and hymns.
Moving about the chakras of the Kalpa and other gardens, languid with intoxication, they satisfy the great Goddess with the honey of their own flowers.
Counted together they are three hundred and sixty. Thus the chakra-deities are the guardians in the seven walls.
Since you asked, they have been told along with the recital of their names. Now I shall tell you the material, extent and power of the other walls as well; take it in.
There are divine mansions set with beryl gems, in which the Nagas and Asuras sport with their women.
Within the great wall called Vaidurya, seven yojanas in, is a wall made of sapphire, like another Chakravala mountain.
The ground of that middle enclosure is made of blue gems, O sage; there are sweet rivers, cool lakes, and various enjoyable and delightful things.
Those mortals on earth who practise Lalita's mantra, at the end of their bodies reach the sapphire enclosure and dwell there.
There, with their women as companions, enjoying divine things, drinking sweet wine and dancing, overflowing with devotion,
by those lakes, on the banks of rivers, O pot-born one, in delightful bowers and very rich mansions,
ever reciting the Goddess's name and reading of her virtues, those fortunate ones dwell surrounded by women.
When their karma is exhausted, they go again to a human body on earth; endowed with their former tendencies, they worship the Chakrini again and go again to the great sapphire region in Shrinagara.
By contact with that very place, O sage, men are always endowed with dark states arising from attachment and aversion.
But those mortals who are wise, free from the pairs of opposites and self-controlled, O sage, filled with wonder, enter into the great Goddess.
Within the wall called Indranila, seven yojanas in, is a wall made of pearls, with gate-towers as before.
The ground between them is exceedingly bright and clear, O sage; all of it is studded with pearls, cool and very charming.
Tamraparni, Mahaparni, ever with pearl-water — such great rivers flow in that great region.
On their banks dwell all the inhabitants of the world of the gods, who in a former birth practised the Goddess's mantra.
In the eight portions beginning with the east are the worlds of Shakra and the other guardians, around the pearl wall, joining the gate regions.
Between the gates of the pearl wall and the sapphire wall, in the eastern part is Shakra's world; in its corner is the land of Agni's world.
In the southern part is Yama's city, where the Lord bearing the staff dwells; everywhere reciting Lalita's mantra, of fierce nature,
upholding her command, with Yama's soldiers led by Chitragupta, he enforces the Goddess's covenant, keeping it hidden.
The evil-doers cursed by Guha, those who hate Lalita, fools devoted to false devotion, the obstinate and exceedingly proud,
stealers of mantras, users of evil mantras, those relying on evil knowledge and sin, atheists, those of sinful habits, killers of living beings for no reason,
haters of women, haters of the world, protectors of heretics — into Kalasutra, Raurava and Kumbhipaka, O pot-born one,
into the terrible Asipatravana, Krimibhaksha, Pratapana, Lalakshepa, Suchivedha and Angarapatana —
into such painful hells, O pot-born one, that mighty one casts them by the Goddess's command.
To his west Nirriti, bearing a sword, abides in the world of the Rakshasas as a worshipper of Lalita.
To its north, between the gates, Varuna always abides in the world of Varuna,
intoxicated from tasting Varuni, white-limbed, riding a fish, ever reciting the Goddess's mantra and practising her sequence of worship.
Binding with nooses those who hate the sight of the Goddess, he leads them down the lower path; he frees her devotees from bondage.
In its northern corner is the very bright world of Vayu; there beings with bodies of wind, ever in great bliss,
perfected ones, divine sages, others who practise control of breath, and other yogins devoted to yoga led by Goraksha dwell.
With them the mighty lord of the winds abides there, O pot-born one, in a wholly distinct form.
Ida, Pingala and Sushumna are his three Shaktis, the lord of the winds, ever languid with the intoxication of wine.
With a banner in hand, seated on a great deer as his mount, devoted to worship, meditation and the ordered rites of Lalita,
surrounded by other Shaktis whose bodies are filled with bliss, the glorious lord of the winds ever recites the name of the Chakrini.
By that power, at the end of the kalpa, he reduces the three worlds with all that moves and does not move to dust, and plays with them in a moment.
For the accomplishment of that power he abides worshipping and meditating on that same Lalita, adorned with all ornaments.
In the eastern part of that world, in the very bright world of the Yakshas, dwells the glorious lord of Yakshas, between the two gates,
with the nine treasures in their forms and with Shaktis led by Riddhi and Vriddhi, filling Lalita's devotees with wealth and prosperity.
With charming, obliging Yaksha women and with various kinds of wine he worships the Chakrini.
Manibhadra, Purnabhadra, Maniman, Manikandhara and others are the commanders of the Yakshas there.
In the eastern part of that world is the glorious world of Rudra, studded with priceless jewels; there Rudra is the presiding deity,
ever blazing with wrath, his great quiver always fastened, with great beings like himself, skilled in sustaining the worlds,
with strung bows, capable, stationed in sixteen enclosures; surrounded by them, he ever recites the Goddess's mantra with his mouths,
accomplished in meditation on the Goddess, eager to worship her, his sides adorned with hosts of many crores of Rudranis.
All of them have blazing limbs, proud of fresh youth, absorbed in meditation on Lalita, ever languid with wine.
With them the glorious Maharudra, bearing the trident, is attended by Hiranyabahu and other Rudras.
Those who have fallen from the sight of Lalita, the arrogant and those who scorn their teachers, he pierces with the tip of his spear, and with the bitter fire from his eyes
he burns them, destroying their wives, servants and offspring; the great hero upholding her command, the protector of Lalita's command,
abides in the exceedingly beautiful world of Rudra, O pot-born one. That Maharudra's attendants, O sage, are the destroyers;
who can tell the countless Rudras? The Rudras who are on the earth by thousands upon thousands,
those in heaven by thousands upon thousands, those whose arrows are food, those whose arrows are the winds,
those whose arrows are the rain, blazing, with tawny eyes, the mighty ones dwelling in the ocean and in the atmosphere,
with matted hair, full of sweetness, blue-necked and red, those who are lords of beings, without arrows and with braided hair,
those who pierce people in food and those drinking from vessels, the Rudras who protect the roads and those who dwell at holy fords,
and other thousands bearing spears and quivers — the Rudras who carry out Lalita's command stand in all directions.
All those great souls, able to bear the three worlds in a moment, compassionate, protect those skilled in meditation on the Goddess, the reciters of her mantra,
and the devotees of the Goddess. In the chakra of sixteen enclosures within the ring of the pearl rampart,
all those Rudras led by Hiranyabahu, resorting to the glorious Maharudra, worship his blazing wrath.
Below are the attendant, the forest lord, and he whose arrows are spears; the lords of those who wish to kill and of those who steal, O pot-born one,
the unbounded, the very wise, the night-rover, O sage, the lord of the elements, the turbaned one, the mountain-dweller,
the lord of the kuluñchas, the bearer of arrows, O pot-born one, the bow-bearer, the stringer, the one who fits the arrow,
and the one who draws — these sixteen dwell in the sixteen-spoked figure; also those who release, who shoot and who pierce, O lord of the ocean,
those seated, lying, moving and waking, standing and running, the members of assemblies and the lords of assemblies,
the horses and the lords of horses, the wounding ones, the piercing ones, the leaders of hosts and the great ones, O crusher of the Vindhya,
and the Gritsas — eighteen kinds of deities in the eighth enclosure. Then the lords of the Gritsas, the troops and lords of troops,
the Ganas and lords of Ganas, those of all forms and of deformed forms, the great and the small, those with chariots and those without,
the chariots and the charioteers, the armies and the army leaders, the attendants, the gatherers, the carpenters and chariot-makers,
and the potters — these Rudras are the deities of the ninth enclosure. The smiths, the Punjishthas, the Nishadas and the arrow-makers,
the bow-makers, the hunters, the dog-keepers and the dogs, the horses and lords of horses, Bhava and Rudra, O pot-born one,
Sharva, Pashupati, Nilagriva, Shitikantha, Kapardin, Vyuptakesha, the thousand-eyed,
Shatadhanva, Girisha, Shipivishta and Midhushtama — these Rudras are declared to be in the tenth wall.
Then in the eleventh chakra are the arrow-bearer, the short one and the dwarf, the great, the eldest, the aged, together with the prosperous,
the foremost, the first, the swift, the quick, the speedy and the rapid, the Rudras of the wave and the calm water, the one of the stream and the divine one,
the eldest and the youngest, the first-born and the last-born, the middle one, the one to be understood and the lowest, O pot-born one —
these twenty-four mighty Rudras are declared. Then Budhnya, Somya Rudra, Pratisarpaka, Yamyaka,
Kshemya, Uvachava, Khalya, then Shlokya, Avasanyaka, Vanya, Kakshya, Shrava, and then another, Pratishrava,
Ashushena, Ashuratha and Shura, O treasure of austerity, Avabhinda, Varmin, Varuthin with Bilmin,
Kavachin, Shruta, Sena and Dundubhya, Ahananya and Dhrishnu — these are remembered as twenty-six; they dwell in the twelfth enclosure, huge-bodied and very mighty.
The bold ones, the messengers, the sent ones, the quiver-bearers, another with a quiver, another with sharp arrows, and in battle
the one with good weapons, the one with a good bow, the praiseworthy, the one of the path, O pot-born one, Kapya, Nadhya, Sudha and Sarasya, O crusher of the Vindhya,
then another, Nadhamana, Veshanta, Kupya, Avadhavarshya, Avarshya, Medhya and Vidyutya,
Idhrya, Atapya, the two Vatyas, Reshmya and another, Vastavya, Vastupa and Soma — these are mighty.
Hear, O sage, of the Rudras in the thirteenth enclosure: the copper-red Rudra, Shanga and Pashupati, O sage,
Ugra, Bhima, the one who kills in front and the one who kills from afar, the slayer and the greater slayer, Vrisha and Harikeshaka,
Tara, Shambhu, Mayobhu, Shankara, Mayaskara, Shiva, Shivatara, Tirthya, Kulya, Parya, Aparya, Prataranar and Uttarana, O sage,
Atarya, Labhya and the sixth, Phenya — these Rudra deities are declared in the fourteenth enclosure.
Sikatya, Pravahya and Irinya, O treasure of austerity, Prapathya, Kimshila and then Kshayana,
Kapardin, Pulastya, Goshthya, Grihya, Talpya, Gehya, Katya, Gahvareshtha and Urudipaka,
Niveshtya, Pantavya, Rathanya, Shukya, Haritya, Lotha, Lopya, Urvya and Surmya, O sage,
Payeya, Parnasha, Vaguramanaka, Abhighna, Nashidu, Prakhidana and Kirika,
and the heart of the gods — these thirty-two Rudra deities abide ever armed, O wise one, in the fifteenth enclosure.
In the sixteenth enclosure, at the gates beginning with the east, are those named Vikshinatka, Vichinvatka and Nirhata,
and the Amivaktas and Nishtaptas, who worship Maharudra. Thus served by thousands of Rudras stationed in the sixteen walls,
Maharudra, who executes Lalita's commands, abides in the north-eastern corner of the pearl wall for the prosperity of the worlds.
These mighty Rudras, numbered as in the Shatarudriya, protect those endowed with devotion to Lalita day and night, and bring obstacles upon those not devoted to Goddess Lalita.
Thus the guardians of the directions led by Shakra, stationed in the pearl wall, perform only the service of Lalita, the supreme Queen.
Then within the wall called pearl, seven yojanas in, is the wall called emerald, four yojanas high,
beautiful with gate-towers and other structures as before. There, in the intermediate directions beginning with the south-east, are the dwellings of the Dandanatha —
four abodes are declared, of the extent of the Mantrini's houses. Those who occupied the tiers of the Geyachakra, king of chariots,
those goddesses in the great war with Bhandasura, keep watch there. All the grounds are beautiful, studded with rows of emeralds,
rich in groves of golden palms and full of all things. All the goddesses there, equal in splendour to the Dandanatha,
move about bearing ploughs and pestles. Countless palm trees are there, variegated with new gold,
with trunks a yojana long and very broad leaves, with golden bark, very glossy, giving good shade and bending with fruit.
From root to top the palms hang with pots of wine; they were made by the artisans for the Dandanatha's pleasure.
Drinking again and again that flood of palm-wine, intoxicated, the chakra-goddesses led by Jrimbhini and the Bhairavas led by Hetuka,
and the seven Nigraha goddesses, dance, overcome with intoxication, wherever the great-eyed Dandini is in the four intermediate directions.
There, in the eastern and other directions, are those equal in splendour to the Goddess — Unmattabhairavi and Svapneshi in every direction.
The dwelling of the Dandanatha there is merely nominal; her abode for service is elsewhere, in the region of the great lotus forest; since that enclosure is very far, her house for service is there.
Then, seven yojanas in from the emerald wall, is a rampart of coral, red as the morning sun.
All the grounds there are made of coral; likewise Brahma, coral-hued, seated on the lotus,
having come from Brahma's world with all the lords of sages, tirelessly for the service of Goddess Lalita,
abides with the progenitors of creatures led by Marichi, O lord of the ocean. The fourteen sciences and thousands of subsidiary sciences,
and the sixty-four arts, embodied and very great, dwelling in the coral rampart in Brahma's world, abide for the prosperity of the worlds by the command of the Goddess Lalita.
Then, within the coral wall, seven yojanas in, at the place of the ruby pavilion, surrounding it on every side, is the world of Vishnu, eager to serve Lalita.
There in the world of Vishnu, Vishnu himself, the eternal Madhava, ever abides in distinct forms — fourfold, tenfold and twelvefold.
The deities of the ten incarnations who were born from the Goddess's nails in the great war with Bhandasura are also in the ruby pavilion.
Compared with the previous enclosures, this enclosure is special: it is merely roofed above with masses of ruby stones.
There, within the enclosure, the god bearing conch, discus and mace, distinguished into twelve forms, guards the directions beginning with the east.
In the east is Keshava with the discus, radiant as gold; in the west Narayana with the conch, like a dark cloud;
Madhava with honey, dark as a blue lotus petal, protects; on the southern side is great Govinda with the bow, radiant as the moon;
in the north Vishnu bearing the plough, like the filaments of a lotus; in the south-east Madhusudana with the pestle, like a lotus;
Trivikrama with sword in hand in the south-west, radiant as fire; Vamana with the thunderbolt in the north-west, bright as the young sun;
Shridhara with the pattisha in the north-east, like a white lotus; Hrishikesha with the mallet, radiant as lightning, in the lower direction;
Padmanabha with the Sharnga bow, radiant as a thousand suns, encircles the ruby pavilion in a sunwise direction.
Bearing all weapons, all-powerful, all-knowing, facing in every direction, like the cochineal insect, noose in hand, the unconquered one,
Damodara, the self of all, overflowing with devotion to Lalita, encircles the ruby pavilion in the reverse direction.
Thus with twelve bodies the lotus-eyed Lord, dwelling in the ruby pavilion, shines in the world of Vishnu.
Then within the wall of various gems, seven yojanas in, is the very charming pavilion called the Thousand-pillared.
Studded and adorned with various gems, the lofty wall there is made of various gems.
One row of a thousand pillars runs across, and there are many such rows of pillars in the four directions;
the roof above is as before, of jewelled wood. There the great world of Shiva watches, shining with radiance.
The twenty-eight Shaiva Agamas are remembered as embodied there, and the excellent ones led by Nandi, Bhringi and Mahakala,
the gods of the twenty-six principles and thousands of elephant-faced ones, in that best of Shiva's worlds, the Thousand-pillared Pavilion.
Ishana, lord of all knowledge, the moon-crested one, protector of Lalita's command and executor of her command,
reciter of Lalita's mantra, ever blissful in mind, with Shaiva vision, for the accomplishment of Lalita's mantra by his devotees,
illuminating that power of intelligence, whose form is great light, most skilled in piercing masses of darkness within and without,
all-knowing and all-doing, abiding in the Thousand-pillared Pavilion, the great god, overflowing with devotion to the Goddess, abides, resorting to those respective walls, O pot-born one.
His very great Shakti is named Mahaprakasha; another Shakti is Chakshushmati, and the goddess Chhaya is remembered as the highest.
Thus surrounded by three beloved Shaktis, ever reciting in his heart the knowledge of Lalita, the great Queen,
illuminating the senses of her devotees to brightness, crushing to the root the net of darkness without and within,
there, in the outpouring of the morning sunlight, shines Martanda Bhairava. Within the great wall of the sun's orb, seven yojanas in,
is the wall made of the moon's orb, four yojanas high, with gate-towers, doors, panels and bars as before.
The whole ground between them is called the Gate of Moonlight.
There at the Gate of Moonlight, having performed very severe austerities, the Moon, born from the eye of Atri, attained radiance.
Here abides the one called Shri Somanatha, of spotless form, the god who destroys the darkness of the three worlds and keeps the world turning,
drinking pure moonlight-nectar from a full cup, surrounded by the Shaktis of the twenty-seven asterisms,
always full in his own form, spotless in his nature — there at the Gate of Moonlight abides the Lord Moon.
With recitations, meditations, hymns and hundreds of worships of Lalita, the Moon, accompanied by Ashvini and the others, passes his time there.
Other Shaktis named Tara are there in thousands, near him; that enclosure is filled with them.
Then within the wall of the moon, seven yojanas in, is the wall called Shringara, four yojanas high,
made as if of Kaustubha gems in the form of chambers of love. Within it the whole ground is the great moat of love.
There in the ring of the moat, filled with the nectar of love, are the Shaktis of love, radiant with various ornaments.
Moving about there in a thousand boats, wild with intoxication, they always worship the flower-armed one seated in a boat.
He, obedient to Lalita's command, bewitches the whole universe with the arrows beginning with Sammohana — all the worlds.
By his power, those who are deluded cannot approach the great lotus forest; but the pure in attire, overflowing with devotion to Lalita, go to the lotus forest with attentive minds.
Gods, Siddhas and men cannot go there; but Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara, pure-minded by nature, go by her command to the great lotus forest.
Worldly people blinded by passion, with many desires and fancies, men of great families darkened by doubtful knowledge,
deep in abundant passion, are not able to cross the great moat of love, which produces intense delusion.
For Smara, of invincible beauty, who bewitches the people of the three worlds, is in charge of the great moat of love.
Having passed beyond all of his enchantment, which bewitches even the great, no one is able to go to the great lotus forest.
Then, within the Shringara wall, seven yojanas in, is the house of the wish-granting gem, the great abode of the Chakraraja.
The whole ground in its midst, adorned with jewels all around, is the great lotus forest, granting all good fortune.
There are gate-towers up to the great Kala wall called Shringara, O sage; the gate-towers are arranged in the same way in all four directions.
In all directions there are a hundred gate-towers, O sage; the auspicious walls are declared to be twenty-five.
The base of every wall measures a yojana. Now I shall describe the lotus-forest region; listen attentively, O sage.
Studded with all jewels, over an extent of six yojanas all around, there are land-lotuses with great stalks.
The stalks are a yojana long, covered with soft thorns; the leaves are ten palm-lengths long.
The filaments of the lotuses are five palm-lengths long, and the pericarps are declared to be ten palm-lengths high.
Exceedingly tender and ever in bloom, charming with fresh fragrance and with broad petals, there are lotuses in multitudes, crores upon crores.
In the eastern part of the great lotus-forest enclosure, O pot-born one, a krosha high, in the form of fire, circular in shape,
half a yojana wide, with ten digits, stands the great support of the offering vessel, O pot-born one.
Around that support, Shaktis with blazing bodies shine — the ten digits of fire, led by Dhumrarchis,
bright with the beauty of youth, adorned with various ornaments; embracing the glorious Lord Fire in the form of the support, they abide all around, languid with love.
Dhumrarchis, Ushna, Jvalini, Jvalini, Visphulingini, Sushri, Surupa, Kapila, Havyavaha and Kavyavaha — these are declared the ten digits of fire in the form of the support.
Upon that support is the god in the form of the vessel: the Sun, whose rising is famed for destroying the darkness of the three worlds.
That vessel, whose nature is the sun, is a yojana and a half high and a yojana in length and breadth, illuminated with great light.
Around that vessel, their bodies clinging to it like dolls, are the twelve digits of exceedingly brilliant radiance.
